findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Trace mitral regurgitation, physiological. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.
echo.impression: Normal cardiac structure and function. Trace mitral regurgitation, physiological.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right Hoover sign, distractible right-sided weakness and a dragging right leg gait
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive signs of functional weakness
action_criteria.rationale: Her sudden right-sided weakness is diagnosed by positive signs incompatible with a lesion (DSM-5 criterion B; Daum 2014); with SLE in the background, the examination decides whether imaging has a stroke-mimic question to answer.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Negative anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I and lupus anticoagulant, with normal C3, C4 and anti-dsDNA
action_criteria.label: Antiphospholipid antibodies, complement and anti-dsDNA
action_criteria.rationale: In SLE, a focal deficit raises antiphospholipid syndrome and active lupus; the antiphospholipid panel, complement and anti-dsDNA answer that named question.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute or chronic infarct and no white matter lesion on a non-contrast brain MRI with DWI
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast, with DWI, for the stroke-mimic question
action_criteria.rationale: Sudden right hemiparesis in a woman with SLE raises an antiphospholipid-related or lupus-related stroke; a non-contrast MRI with DWI 48 hours after onset answers it once.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Minor QT effect of hydroxychloroquine with sertraline noted; no medicine to stop
action_criteria.label: Review her medicines for interactions (optional)
action_criteria.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine with sertraline has a minor additive QT effect; nothing on her list worsens the deficit or needs tapering.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of the comorbid symptoms that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of comorbidity (optional)
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can quantify her low mood and anxiety to plan treatment; it costs more than any other step on this pathway and adds nothing to the diagnosis, which rests on the examination.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background reading only; no result in it changes this patient's diagnosis or plan
action_criteria.label: Literature search on FND diagnosis and treatment (background, not a clinical step)
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on the positive diagnosis and treatment of functional neurological disorder; it is not part of this patient's diagnostic pathway and earns no credit (round ruling 5).

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
Start corticosteroids or escalate immunosuppression for presumed neuropsychiatric lupus.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional limb weakness, right side) based on the right Hoover sign, distractibility and the dragging right leg gait, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid depression.
Inform her rheumatologist of the admission and the diagnosis, and continue hydroxychloroquine unchanged.

avoided_actions.rationale: No palpitations, syncope or cardiac history; the deficit is not a cardiac question, and the QT effect of her medicines is minor at these doses.
With a normal DWI MRI and positive functional signs there is no embolic stroke to explain, so echocardiography has no question to answer.
No infarct, palpitations or syncope; rhythm monitoring for an embolic source has no question to answer.
At 48 hours the stroke-mimic question is answered by MRI with DWI; a CT adds radiation and no answer.
No question in her right-sided weakness that PET could answer.
Right hemiparesis with a positive Hoover sign, normal reflexes and no wasting is not neuromuscular; a normal EMG reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Right hemisensory loss split exactly at the midline is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — right-sided functional hemimotor syndrome, in patient with quiescent SLE (neuropsychiatric SLE excluded)

differential.key_features: SLE raises it, but the disease is quiescent (no rash, arthritis, fever or renal symptoms), C3, C4 and anti-dsDNA are normal, antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant are negative, and the brain MRI shows no infarct or white matter lesion.

Sudden right hemiparesis raised it, but there is no restricted diffusion 48 hours after onset, reflexes are symmetric without Babinski, and the weakness shows a positive Hoover sign and distractibility.

key_clinical_evidence: Positive signs of functional weakness: right Hoover sign, weakness that improves with distraction and a dragging right leg gait.
She drags the right leg on examination but walks normally to the restroom when unaware of being observed (supportive, low specificity).
The non-contrast brain MRI with DWI shows no infarct or white matter lesion 48 hours after onset.
SLE is serologically quiescent and antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant are negative.
Depression and the failed rotation are supportive context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions also flare with stress. A stressor is supportive context, neither required nor sufficient; the positive signs make the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Onset after a failed clinical rotation and fear of dismissal
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Organic disease and FND can coexist. Her SLE is quiescent, the antiphospholipid and lupus serology is negative, DWI shows no infarct, and the weakness has positive functional signs.
red_herrings.data_point: Established SLE, a mother with SLE, and the patient's own concern about CNS lupus
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on neuropsychiatric lupus and escalate immunosuppression, or pursue lumbar puncture and angiography

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first: its positive signs decide whether imaging has a specific question to answer (Espay 2018).

findings.result: Right hip extension weak on direct testing, full strength during left hip flexion against resistance.
The right arm and leg weakness varies during the examination and improves with distraction.
The right leg is dragged on walking.
Right hemisensory loss stopping exactly at the midline with intact vibration, and normal walking to the restroom when unaware of being observed; not counted as rule-in signs.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: right Hoover sign, distractibility of the right-sided weakness and a dragging right leg gait. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion.

interactions: Hydroxychloroquine + sertraline: both can prolong the QT interval; at these doses, without other QT risk factors, the risk is low. No pharmacokinetic interaction.
general.proposed: Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily; Sertraline 100 mg once daily
general.summary: Minor additive QT effect of hydroxychloroquine with sertraline; no contraindicated combination.
warnings: Hydroxychloroquine: retinal toxicity with long-term use; keep the daily dose at or below 5 mg/kg actual body weight, with annual retinal screening after 5 years of use.
Sertraline: hyponatremia from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; bleeding risk with antiplatelet drugs, anticoagulants or NSAIDs.

labs.interpretation: ESR 22 mm/hr (mildly high). Remaining results within reference ranges; antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant negative.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

Major intracranial vessels demonstrate normal flow voids

signal_characteristics.T2_FLAIR: No white matter or cortical signal abnormality

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Functional right-sided weakness in a woman with SLE who fears CNS lupus. The examination gives a Hoover sign, distractibility and a dragging gait; the comorbidity earns one non-contrast MRI with DWI and a targeted antiphospholipid and lupus serology panel, both normal, and the trap is to treat presumed neuropsychiatric lupus.
metadata.notes: Moderate FND: right-sided functional weakness in a patient with quiescent SLE. The named question is neuropsychiatric lupus or antiphospholipid-related stroke, answered once by DWI MRI and the antiphospholipid and lupus serology.
metadata.revision_reason: October 2026 review round: brain MRI and targeted SLE serology recommended for the named stroke-mimic question; criteria, outputs and assessment rebuilt to the FND criteria pack tiers.

family_history: No family history of neurological disease
past_medical_history: Lupus (SLE) — quiescent, established diagnosis 4 years ago

social_history.recent_stressor: Failed clinical rotation assessment 3 weeks ago; concern about being dismissed from nursing program

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. W is a 29-year-old nursing student with established quiescent SLE who presents with 48 hours of right-sided arm and leg weakness and right hemisensory loss. She has had SLE for 4 years, managed with hydroxychloroquine, with no prior major organ involvement and quiescent disease activity for 18 months. Her rheumatologist last assessed her 3 months ago and found the disease quiescent. The neurological symptoms began abruptly 48 hours ago without any prodrome. She has been in good health and her SLE has been well-controlled. She failed a clinical rotation assessment 3 weeks ago and is concerned about dismissal from her nursing program. Her nursing training makes her familiar with lupus cerebritis, antiphospholipid syndrome, and CNS vasculitis, and she is worried about CNS lupus involvement. She has no prior neurological presentations. She has no fever, no joint pain flare, no rash, and no renal symptoms. She denies headache. On directed questioning, she acknowledges significant stress from the nursing program failure and feels her symptoms began after a particularly difficult study session.

neurological_exam.additional: Witnessed during examination: right-sided weakness and sensory findings as above; no involuntary movements or seizure-like episodes observed.
neurological_exam.coordination: Normal left side. Cannot fully test right due to apparent weakness.
neurological_exam.gait: Right leg dragging. Observed to walk normally to restroom when unaware of observation.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Anxious. Demonstrates good medical knowledge from nursing training.
neurological_exam.motor: Right arm weakness 3/5 on formal testing. Right leg: hip extension weak on direct testing but full during left hip flexion against resistance (positive Hoover sign on the right). Weakness varies during the examination and improves with distraction. No wasting.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Normal 2+ symmetric. No Babinski. No pathological reflexes.
neurological_exam.sensory: Right-sided sensory loss — stops exactly at midline. Vibration intact throughout.
